summary: Describes a framework for using YANG data models to automate the management of services and networks over their life cycle. Models can produce configuration for components and describe the state to monitor, helping with tasks such as service instantiation and provisioning.

plainLanguage.summary: A big-picture guide to using standard descriptions of networks so computers can set up and watch over services automatically.

questions: how to automate network management with yang
how to automate network service delivery
how to implement multi-layer network models
subtitle: How to use standardized data descriptions to automate service delivery and network management.

tldr.problem: Network operators manage services using separate systems (OSS, BSS, operations centers) that speak different data languages. Manual configuration and limited visibility make service delivery slow, error-prone, and hard to scale.
tldr.mechanism: YANG data models organized in three layers (service, network, device) provide a shared language. Service models describe what customers want; network models translate this into technology-specific tasks; device models handle individual equipment configuration. Mapping between layers automates the entire service lifecycle from provisioning through monitoring and diagnosis.
tldr.outcome: Multi-vendor networks can be automated end-to-end. Configuration, monitoring, and closed-loop optimization become programmatic. Services respond dynamically to network changes and performance feedback.

today: RFC 8969 is an Informational document that describes the framework and provides examples. It builds on RFC 8309 (Service Models Explained) and references numerous YANG module specifications for service models (L2VPN, L3VPN, virtual networks) and device models (BGP, QoS, routing, interfaces). The framework is a guide for how to develop and integrate YANG models across multiple layers; it does not define new YANG modules itself.

sections.title: The Automation Problem and Solution
sections.content:
Traditional network management requires manual handoffs between teams. A customer orders a service, the order goes to a design team, then to a provisioning team, then to operations. Each team uses different tools and speaks a different language (databases, proprietary APIs, CLI commands). Adding new services or vendors requires extensive custom integration.

YANG (RFC 7950) is a language for describing data structures in a vendor-neutral way. This framework proposes using YANG data models to automate the entire service lifecycle: exposure (letting customers request services), creation (provisioning the request), assurance (monitoring that it works), optimization (improving performance), diagnosis (troubleshooting problems), and decommission (removing the service).

The key insight is to organize YANG modules in layers. A service model describes what a customer needs (bandwidth, latency, VPN membership). A network model translates this into operator-facing concepts (tunnels, route distinguishers, traffic engineering). Device models handle technology-specific details (BGP configuration, QoS rules, interface settings). Mapping between layers automates the translation.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of teams manually configuring each device, one data model describes what the service should do, and software automatically figures out what each router needs.

sections.title: The Three-Layer Model
sections.content:
Service models capture customer-facing requirements using top-down design. They describe connectivity needs (pipe for point-to-point, hose for one-to-many, funnel for many-to-one), traffic guarantees (latency, loss, available bandwidth), security (which sites can reach each other), and notifications (alerts when SLA is breached). Service models are technology-agnostic; a customer does not specify 'use MPLS' or 'use BGP', just 'I need 50 Mbps with 20 ms latency.'

Network models translate service requirements into operator-specific infrastructure views. A service model requesting an L3 VPN becomes a network model describing how to build it: which PE routers to use, which route distinguishers and route targets to apply, which tunnels to establish. Network models span multiple devices and multiple layers of technology.

Device models describe individual device configuration, typically technology-specific and following a bottom-up design. Examples include BGP peer configuration, ACL rules, QoS profiles, interface settings, and MPLS labels. Many device models already exist in IETF standards.

An orchestrator lives at the service layer, managing requests and mapping them to network models. A controller lives at the network/device layer, translating network models into device configurations. This layering allows reuse: the same device models can support many different service models through different mappings.
sections.plainLanguage: Customers describe what they want, a middle layer figures out how the network should work, and a low layer tells individual devices what to do.

sections.title: Service Lifecycle Management
sections.content:
A YANG-based framework handles the complete service lifecycle automatically.

Exposure and creation: A service catalog (built from service models) shows customers what services are available and what parameters they can request. When a customer submits a request, the orchestrator validates it (checking that sufficient resources exist), then maps it to network models and device configurations. Service modifications (adding a new customer site, increasing bandwidth) follow the same flow.

Assurance and optimization: Performance telemetry (latency, loss, jitter) is modeled in YANG and collected continuously. The orchestrator compares actual performance to SLA objectives. If performance degrades, the system can trigger optimization: policy changes, tunnel reoptimization, or capacity reallocation. This creates a closed loop where the service continuously self-adjusts.

Diagnosis and decommission: Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) functions are modeled in YANG as technology-independent RPC operations (for example, 'verify reachability to this address') or technology-dependent procedures (for example, Bidirectional Forwarding Detection). When a problem is detected (through monitoring or customer report), these operations help isolate and fix it. When a customer cancels a service, the orchestrator removes all associated configurations and releases resources.
sections.plainLanguage: The system automatically sets up the service, monitors whether it works, fixes problems, and cleans up when done.

sections.title: Service Decomposition and Mapping
sections.content:
The mapping from service to network to device models is the critical automation step. Service mapping translates high-level service parameters into network-specific configuration. For an L3VPN service requesting a 'pipe' (point-to-point) with guaranteed latency, the mapping creates network model parameters: specific PE routers as ingress and egress, a route distinguisher and route target for isolation, a traffic-engineered tunnel for the latency guarantee.

Service decomposition further breaks down network models into device models. The L3NM (L3 VPN Network Model) is decomposed into BGP configuration, QoS rules, network instance definitions, and interface setup across all involved devices. A router may receive multiple pieces of configuration from different ASAs: the BGP ASA configures peering, the QoS ASA configures traffic classes, the interface ASA configures physical ports.

These mappings can be implemented using the YANG Schema Mount mechanism (RFC 8528), which allows a controller to compose multiple device models within a network model, validating them as a unit and loading them atomically into devices.

Policies defined at service or network layers (for example, 'exclude routes through AS 65000') are translated to device-level policies (BGP policy rules). Notifications and alarms can be similarly tied: an SLA breach at the service layer triggers specific monitoring at the network layer, which triggers device-level OAM operations.
sections.plainLanguage: Software translates service requests step-by-step through network concepts down to device commands, creating a chain that can be updated automatically.

sections.title: Real-World Examples
sections.content:
L2VPN/L3VPN delivery: A customer requests a Layer 3 VPN connecting two sites. The orchestrator maps this to an L3NM specifying route distinguishers, route targets, and tunnel types. The controller decomposes this into BGP configuration (establishing VPN membership), QoS configuration (applying service-level guarantees), interface configuration (on PE devices facing the customer), and addressing configuration (on device interfaces). As network conditions change, telemetry feeds back to the service layer, enabling automatic optimization of tunnel paths or capacity allocation.

Virtual Network (VN) lifecycle: A customer orders a virtual network spanning multiple data centers. The orchestrator works with the TE (Traffic Engineering) topology model to plan paths and create tunnels. The customer negotiates the VN topology and explicit paths using TE models. Telemetry from tunnels (latency, loss) is collected and fed back to the orchestrator for assurance and optimization. If a tunnel fails, the system can automatically reroute or alert the customer via notification models.

Event-driven device management: A device implements an Event-Condition-Action (ECA) policy where it monitors its own state and takes local actions when conditions are met. For example: 'If CPU exceeds 80%, then issue a notification and trigger throttling.' The controller pushes ECA policies to devices, and devices execute autonomously, reducing the need for constant centralized control.
sections.plainLanguage: Real networks use this approach to set up VPN services automatically, manage virtual networks across data centers, and let devices react to problems on their own.

sections.title: Security and Trust
sections.content:
Network management traffic carries sensitive data (customer topologies, traffic patterns, SLA details) and controls critical infrastructure, so security is essential.

NETCONF (RFC 6241) and RESTCONF (RFC 8040) are the standard protocols for delivering YANG models to devices. Both require secure transport: NETCONF mandates SSH, RESTCONF mandates HTTPS/TLS. Access control is enforced using the NETCONF Access Control Model (RFC 8341), which restricts which users can access which data and operations.

When translating between service, network, and device layers, care must be taken to prevent information leakage. A device controller should not expose raw network model details to customers, and service-layer parameters should not be visible to devices operating below them. Authorization and authentication checks ensure data is available only to entitled parties.

Continuous monitoring (Section 4.1.4) helps detect and correct misalignment between layers. If device configuration drifts from the intended network model, or the network model deviates from service objectives, automated checks and service diagnosis functions can identify and report the problem.
sections.plainLanguage: All communication is encrypted and authenticated. Each layer of the system only sees the data it needs, and automated checks catch configuration mistakes.
